papers.title: Study protocol for a prospective multicenter longitudinal cohort study on progression of moderate aortic valve stenosis, the MODAS Study
papers.abstract: Background: Calcific aortic stenosis (AS) is one of the most common and prognostically relevant valvular heart diseases, with a growing global burden driven by population ageing. Prediction of disease progression from moderate to severe AS, which would be instrumental for earlier diagnosis and treatment, remains challenging. At the same time, moderate AS is increasingly recognized as a heterogeneous condition associated with clinically relevant risk, particularly in patients with cardiac damage, heart failure, or rapid disease progression. Conventional echocardiographic parameters incompletely capture the biological heterogeneity underlying AS progression. The MODAS study was established to investigate biomarkers and mechanisms of AS progression and outcome using longitudinal multimodal phenotyping. Methods: The MODAS Study is a prospective, multicenter, longitudinal observational cohort study enrolling adults with moderate calcific tricuspid AS at three tertiary heart valve centers in Germany. Participants undergo standardized baseline assessment including clinical phenotyping, laboratory testing, electrocardiography, transthoracic echocardiography, cardiac computed tomography and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. Biospecimens are collected for biomarker, immunologic, proteomic, and genetic analyses, including genome-wide association studies and assessment of clonal haematopoiesis. Participants are followed annually for up to 5 years with repeat clinical assessment, laboratory testing, and echocardiography. The primary endpoint is time to progression to severe AS according to 2025 ESC/EACTS guideline criteria or aortic valve replacement for severe AS, adjudicated by the local multidisciplinary Heart Team. Secondary endpoints include all-cause mortality and additional clinical outcome trajectories. Multimodal data integration will be used to develop and validate prediction models for disease progression and outcome. Discussion: The MODAS Study will provide a harmonized, deeply phenotyped longitudinal dataset to improve risk stratification in moderate AS and to identify imaging, inflammatory, and genetic markers associated with rapid progression and adverse outcomes. The study is designed to support future personalized surveillance strategies, improved selection for earlier intervention, and mechanistic understanding of calcific AS progression. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05851209. Registered on 9 May 2023.

papers.title: A transient decrease in night-to-night variability of REM sleep before myocardial infarction
papers.abstract: Background. Myocardial infarction (MI) outcomes depend on time to treatment, and fatigue and sleep disturbance are often reported in the weeks before the event. Whether wearable-measured sleep changes within individuals before MI, and whether such change is specific to MI, is unknown. Methods. In the All of Us Research Program, adults with a first MI code and at least 180 valid Fitbit sleep nights in the preceding 360 days were matched to up to 10 controls on sex, comorbidities, sleep apnea, calendar time and a propensity score. The full matched cohort of all cases was the primary cohort, and cases with diabetes and/or hypertension formed a subgroup. The main endpoints were the within-person change in night-to-night variability (SD, RMSSD, CV) of the REM-sleep fraction at days 30-16 relative to each persons baseline (days 360-121) and from days 30-16 to days 15-1, tested against 10,000 randomly placed index dates with allowance for the choice of window (max-T). The same pipeline was applied to cases without recorded symptoms or treatment, to an index date at the first angina code, to a cohort including heart failure and to ischaemic stroke and admissions for heart failure, pneumonia, fracture or appendicitis and any cause, and the analysis was adjusted for nightly heart rate, wear and device. Results. The full matched cohort comprised 45 cases and 450 controls. REM-fraction variability changed transiently before MI, decreasing at days 30-16 and returning towards baseline over days 15-1; allowing for the choice of window, this decrease-then-return pattern was rarely matched at 10,000 randomly placed index dates (max-T p<0.001). Its components were the decrease in SD at days 30-16 (Cliffs {delta} -0.30, p=0.004; OR per SD 0.53, 95% CI 0.35-0.80; max-T p=0.0034) and the return in RMSSD over days 15-1 ({delta} +0.36, p<0.001; max-T p=0.0035); day by day, the decrease was not detected as a continuous change (cluster permutation test p=0.58). The decrease in SD was not seen at the same time before admissions for pneumonia (69 cases), fracture or appendicitis (130) or any cause (859) and was larger before MI than before each of them (difference in {delta} -0.25 to -0.34), whereas the rise over days 15-1 was shared with pneumonia; it was of similar size in the subgroup with diabetes and/or hypertension, in cases without recorded symptoms or treatment, with the index date at the first angina code, when people with heart failure were included and after adjustment for nightly heart rate, wear and device. Scoring each person against their own baseline discriminated cases from controls with AUCs of up to 0.66, probably an optimistic estimate because the decrease in RMSSD was attenuated in held-out halves of the matched sets. Conclusions. In adults who use consumer wearables, a first MI was preceded by a transient change in night-to-night REM-sleep variability, a decrease at days 30-16 and a return over the following two weeks. The decrease was not seen at the same time before other acute admissions, did not depend on recorded symptoms or treatment and was detectable against each persons own baseline with simple measures. The timing is an exploratory finding, to be confirmed in new cases.

papers.title: Distinct Biomarker Signatures of CMR-Defined Myocardial Remodeling in Moderate Aortic Stenosis
papers.abstract: Background: Moderate aortic stenosis (AS) is associated with adverse outcomes, yet the myocardial response to pressure overload varies substantially between patients and is incompletely reflected by valve hemodynamics. We aimed to determine whether circulating biomarkers of myocardial stress, injury, and fibrosis associate with cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR)-defined myocardial remodeling in moderate AS. Methods: Eighty-nine patients with moderate AS prospectively underwent CMR (cine imaging, T1 mapping, extracellular volume fraction [ECV], late gadolinium enhancement [LGE]) with concurrent measurement of NT-proBNP, high-sensitivity troponin T, sST2, TIMP-1, and Galectin-3. Biomarker associations with the phenotype-defining CMR parameters were tested with adjustment for age, sex, and renal function and correction for multiple testing, and patients were additionally classified into 4 hierarchical remodeling phenotypes. Results: Six of 20 biomarker-CMR associations remained significant after correction for multiple testing. NT-proBNP tracked LV mass index (beta=0.50), ECV (beta=0.35), and LGE burden (beta=0.43, all q<0.05). TIMP-1 and Galectin-3 were selectively associated with native T1 (both beta=0.35, q=0.012), and sST2 was inversely associated with LV mass index (beta=-0.27, q=0.046). TIMP-1 (adjusted OR 2.18 per SD, 95% CI 1.37-3.48, q=0.005) and NT-proBNP (OR 2.10, 1.19-3.69, q=0.026) increased with higher hierarchical remodeling phenotype. No biomarker was associated with echocardiographic mean gradient, peak velocity, or indexed valve area after correction. Conclusions: Circulating biomarkers showed distinct associations with CMR measures of myocardial remodeling in moderate AS. Matrix-related biomarkers were associated with native T1, whereas NT-proBNP was associated across several remodeling domains. These signals were not measurably related to valve hemodynamics.

papers.title: Multi-Model Comparison of Deep and Classical Architectures for ECG Diagnostic Superclass Classification on PTB-XL
papers.abstract: Which architecture is best for sorting 12-lead ECGs into diagnostic superclasses still remains somewhat unsettled in the literature. In this study we compared six different models on PTB-XL (21,375 records) under one single patient-level split: a Mamba-style state space model (M1), a 1D residual CNN (M2), a BiLSTM (M3), a CRNN with attention (M4), a soft-voting ensemble of M2 to M4 (M5), and MiniRocket features with LightGBM (M6). Each record was labeled with the superclass of its highest-likelihood diagnostic code. We then scored the saved per-record predictions with paired patient-level bootstrap intervals, McNemar tests, per-class AUROC and AUPRC, sensitivity, specificity, and calibration. The ensemble reached the highest macro F1 (0.665, 95% CI 0.644-0.685), ahead of every single deep model by 0.020-0.041 (all paired CIs excluded zero) and ahead of M6 (0.645) by 0.021 (95% CI 0.002-0.040). We chose its members after seeing test results, so these margins are optimistic: ensembles built from validation-selected members, or from all four deep models, scored 0.656-0.657, about 0.009 lower (paired CIs included zero). M5 and M6 did not differ significantly in accuracy, and their macro AUROC was nearly identical (0.916 and 0.914). M1 trailed M2 and M3 by 0.021. Hypertrophy (HYP) was the hardest class (F1 0.33-0.41). Differences in HYP recall mostly reflected where each model's threshold sat: M6 had the lowest recall but the highest AUROC (0.871). We used only a single dataset and split, with no pretraining and no external validation, and so these results do not show that any model is ready for clinical use.

papers.title: Integrated multiomic scores for cardiovascular disease prediction across multiancestral populations
papers.abstract: Background: Genomic, epigenomic, and proteomic data capture complementary aspects of cardiovascular disease biology, but the value of integrating these data for predicting multiple cardiovascular disease outcomes across ancestry groups remains uncertain. Methods: We derived disease-specific proteomic scores using 999 plasma proteins in 50,673 UK Biobank participants and validated them in 9,358 participants from the Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiological (PURE) study. In PURE, we integrated these proteomic scores with 2,279 polygenic scores and 479 DNA methylation scores to develop 4 multiomic scores (MEGASCOREs) for myocardial infarction (MI), atrial fibrillation (AF), heart failure (HF), and cardiovascular mortality. Associations with incident cardiovascular disease, discrimination, calibration, and performance across ancestry groups were evaluated in PURE and 2 additional cohorts. Results: In pooled analyses, each standard deviation increase in the corresponding MEGASCORE was associated with MI (hazard ratio [HR], 2.13; 95% CI, 1.86-2.43), AF (HR, 1.94; 95% CI, 1.68-2.24), HF (HR, 3.33; 95% CI, 2.75-4.05), and cardiovascular mortality (HR, 3.28; 95% CI, 2.33-4.61). MEGASCOREs improved discrimination compared with clinical models, with strongest improvements for HF and cardiovascular mortality. MEGASCORE-CV-Death had a higher area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) than SCORE2 for cardiovascular mortality (0.83 [95% CI, 0.82-0.85] vs. 0.78 [95% CI, 0.77-0.80]). Its discrimination was also higher than that of SCORE2 across all 4 ancestry groups, with better calibration across non-European ancestry groups. MEGASCOREs remained associated with cardiovascular outcomes among participants without conventional cardiovascular risk factors. Conclusions: Integrated multiomic MEGASCOREs were associated with multiple cardiovascular outcomes and provided prognostic information beyond conventional clinical variables in PURE.

papers.title: Ultra-high-resolution Photon-Counting CT for Leaflet-Specific Evaluation of Fibrosis and Calcification in Aortic Stenosis
papers.abstract: Objectives: Ultra-high-resolution photon-counting detector (PCD)-CT may enable leaflet-specific analysis of aortic valve fibrosis and calcification, providing insights into early aortic stenosis (AS) disease progression. This study aimed to investigate how PCD-CT leaflet-specific calcific and fibrotic volumes influence cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) leaflet mobility. Materials and methods: Participants with moderate aortic AS prospectively underwent both PCD-CT (n=80) and CMR (n=58). Using PCD-CT, calcific and fibrotic volumes were segmented for right (RCC), left (LCC), and non-coronary cusps (NCC) and indexed to the aortic annulus area (ICV and IFV). CMR-derived leaflet mobility index (LMI) was assessed. Two raters compared image quality using a Likert scale (1=poor to 5=excellent) and distinguishability of individual leaflets in PCD-CT with EID-CT (n=82). Results: PCD-CT analysis showed that calcification was higher in males (e.g., ICVRCC: 15+/-16 vs. 4+/-7 uL/cm^2; p<0.001), while fibrosis was higher in females (e.g., IFVLCC: 47+/-18 vs. 34+/-15 uL/cm^2; p=0.004) across all leaflets. Fibrocalcific ratio was higher in LCC (53+/-276) compared to RCC (19+/-48; p<0.001) and NCC (13.5+/-34; p<0.001). LMI of RCC was higher in females compared to men (0.66+/-0.21 vs. 0.38+/-0.33; p=0.008). LMILCC and LMINCC showed no sex differences. LMIRCC negatively correlated with ICVRCC ({rho}=-0.64 [-0.77, -0.46]; p<0.001) and LMINCC with ICVNCC ({rho}=-0.69 [-0.80, -0.53]; p<0.001), whereas LMILCC negatively correlated with IFVLCC ({rho}=-0.35 [-0.56, -0.10]; p=0.007), particularly in females ({rho}=-0.70 [-0.89, -0.31]; p=0.003). PCD-CT yielded higher image quality (5 [IQR 4-5] vs. 3 [3-4]; p<0.001) and leaflet distinguishability (79/80 [99%] vs. 42/82 [51%]; p<0.001) than EID-CT. Conclusions: Ultra-high-resolution PCD-CT allows for leaflet-specific quantification of indexed fibrotic and calcific volume. These volumes demonstrate sex- and leaflet-specific differences that may distinctly contribute to AS pathophysiology.

papers.title: Stage-dependent associations of Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome with Cognitive Decline, Depression, and Neuroimaging Signatures in multi-regional older adults
papers.abstract: Background Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) syndrome is a multisystem condition associated with adverse outcomes, yet its impact on age-related cognitive health remains understudied. We examined associations of CKM with neurocognitive and neuropsychiatric outcomes, modifiable physical and psychosocial factors contributing to cognitive impairment across CKM stages, and neuroimaging correlates. Methods Global aging cohorts (mean follow-up 6.5 years) and the Cohort Studies of Memory in an International Consortium (5.4 years) were used. CKM stages (0-4) were defined according to AHA framework. Longitudinal domain-specific cognitive changes were assessed using linear mixed-effects models, and depressive symptoms using generalized linear regression with individual participant data approach. Population-attributable fractions were estimated for six modifiable factors associated with cognitive impairment across CKM stages. Cross-sectional associations with 34 neuroimaging biomarkers were examined in UK Biobank. Results Among 28,242 participants, advanced CKM stages (3-4) were associated with accelerated cognitive decline, particularly in attention, executive function, and language. Associations were stronger in younger individuals, men, and those with less education, but not modified by APOE 4 status. Advanced CKM stages were associated with depressive symptoms among cognitively unimpaired individuals. Modifiable factors accounted for 24.8% of cognitive impairment risk across CKM stages, mainly social isolation (7.0%), depressive symptoms (5.2%), and physical inactivity (5.2%). Advanced CKM stages were linked to widespread MRI alterations (27 biomarkers), especially white matter hyperintensity. Conclusion Advanced CKM stages are associated with accelerated cognitive decline and greater cerebrovascular burden. Addressing psychosocial factors and physical inactivity, alongside management of CKM risk factors, may help reduce cognitive impairment.

papers.title: Dual-Energy Pulsed Field and Radiofrequency Ablation With a Contact Force-Sensing Focal Catheter for Ventricular Arrhythmias: Initial Clinical Experience
papers.abstract: Background. Clinical data on ventricular ablation with a contact force-sensing focal catheter capable of delivering both radiofrequency (RF) and pulsed field (PF) energy are limited. Objective. To describe the procedural characteristics, acute efficacy, and safety of dual-energy ablation with the Dual Energy THERMOCOOL SMARTTOUCH SF (DE-STSF) catheter in consecutive patients with ventricular arrhythmias. Methods. This observational single-center study included all consecutive patients who underwent catheter ablation of premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) or ventricular tachycardia (VT) with the DE-STSF catheter between June and October 2026. Results. Twenty-six patients were included (median age 65.5 [55.8-71.0] years; 77% male; median left ventricular ejection fraction 44.0% [30.0-53.8]). Eighteen underwent VT ablation, including 10 with electrical storm or incessant VT and 6 with prior VT ablation; 8 underwent PVC ablation. All patients received RF followed by PF consolidation. Noninducibility of any sustained VT or ventricular fibrillation was achieved in 16/18 VT patients (89%), and acute PVC elimination in all 8 PVC patients. No major procedure-related complications were documented during hospitalization. During a median follow-up of 68 [47-82] days, VT recurred in 2 patients; of whom one patient underwent repeat endocardial and epicardial ablation. No PVC recurrences were documented. Conclusion. In this initial clinical experience, sequential RF and PF ablation using a single contact force-sensing catheter proved feasible for the treatment of ventricular arrhythmias, achieving high acute success with a favorable early safety profile. Whether PF consolidation confers incremental benefit beyond RF ablation alone warrants prospective comparative evaluation.

papers.title: Health Literacy and Cardiovascular Health Among Formerly Incarcerated Individuals: Evidence from the JUSTICE Study
papers.abstract: Background: Health literacy, defined as the ability to find, understand, and use health information, is a key determinant of cardiovascular disease but remains underexamined among individuals transitioning from incarceration to community life. This study examined the association between health literacy and cardiovascular health among adults recently released from incarceration. Methods: Using baseline data from the Justice-Involved Individuals Cardiovascular Disease Epidemiology (JUSTICE) study, a prospective cohort of individuals with cardiovascular risk factors released from correctional facilities, we examined the association between health literacy, as measured by the Short Test of Functional Health Literacy in Adults, and cardiovascular health, as measured by the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 (LE8). Results: Among 439 participants (mean age 45 years), 32 (7%) demonstrated inadequate health literacy. Hispanic ethnicity (53% vs. 25%), less than high school education (50% vs. 20%), and homelessness (16% vs. 3.2%) were significantly associated with inadequate health literacy. In bivariate analyses, inadequate health literacy was associated with lower LE8 blood glucose (63.1 vs. 76.8, p = 0.02), and LE8 physical activity (19.4 vs. 32.2, p = 0.03), but higher LE8 diet (55.5 vs. 43.8, p = 0.04) scores. After adjusting for age, gender, race/ethnicity, education level, and housing status, inadequate health literacy remained independently associated with lower LE8 glucose scores ({beta} = -11.9, 95% CI: -22.9 to -0.8, p = 0.04). Conclusion: Health literacy is a modifiable determinant of cardiovascular health, particularly glycemic control, in justice-involved populations. Interventions strengthening health literacy may help reduce health disparities among formerly incarcerated individuals.

papers.title: Polygenic risk and genomic signals in premature coronary artery disease
papers.abstract: Background: Premature coronary artery disease (pCAD) is a distinct presentation of CAD. Using the All of Us (AoU) Research Program data, we compared pCAD with later-onset CAD across cardiometabolic, polygenic, and genome-wide domains. Methods: We conducted a retrospective, cross-sectional case-case analysis of All of Us Research Program (AoU) participants with established CAD. pCAD was defined as first CAD event before age 55 years in males and before age 65 in females; later-onset CAD was defined as the first CAD event at or after age threshold. Pre-index cardiometabolic measures were extracted from electronic health records and modelled with logistic regression. Using 607,719 variants, a CAD polygenic risk score (PRS) was constructed using published summary statistics and short-read whole-genome sequencing data (srWGS). Results were standardized within self-reported race groups, and evaluated overall, by race, and with a PRS x race interaction. A case-case genome-wide association study (GWAS) compared pCAD with later-onset CAD. Results: The CAD cohort included 49,919 participants, including 18,455 with pCAD and 31,464 with later-onset CAD. Participants with pCAD had higher BMI, LDL cholesterol and diastolic blood pressure, and lower HDL cholesterol, serum calcium, and systolic blood pressure. Higher BMI and LDL cholesterol were positively associated with higher odds of pCAD, whereas higher HDL cholesterol, systolic blood pressure, and serum calcium were inversely associated. PRS was associated with greater odds of pCAD in the genomic models (OR per 1-SD higher PRS, 1.14; 95% CI, 1.12?1.17; P<0.001). Analyses stratified by race showed PRS association was present among White participants but was not observed among Black participants. In the case-case GWAS, one variant reached genome-wide significance at 2q24.3 (rs13383835; OR=1.20; 95% CI, 1.13-1.27; P=5.8x10-9). A total of 137 variants met an exploratory threshold of P<1x10-5. Conclusions: Premature onset of CAD is characterized by a distinct cardiometabolic profile driven by modifiable risk factors, greater polygenic burden, and genomic signals associated with earlier disease timing. A European-derived PRS did not transfer to Black participants, who were overrepresented in pCAD. Together, these findings support pCAD as a clinically and genetically distinct presentation of CAD and highlight the need for ancestry-specific validation of genomic risk tools in diverse cohorts.

papers.title: Urban, regional and remote outcomes following TAVR for Queensland patients: a retrospective cohort study
papers.abstract: Background Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) offers a minimally invasive approach to treat severe aortic stenosis (AS) but can only be performed at centres meeting strict regulatory requirements. It remains unclear whether this requirement restricts TAVR access for patients residing in rural Australia, and whether such people experience poorer outcomes than metropolitan counterparts as a result. Methods This multicentre retrospective cohort study used Australian Cardiac Outcomes Registry data. All Queensland residents who underwent TAVR between April 2018 and 27 March 2026 were included. Rurality was assigned by postcode using the Modified Monash Model (MMM) and grouped as urban (MMM1), regional (MMM2-4), or remote (MMM5-7). The primary outcome was 12-month mortality and was investigated using Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards analyses. Findings Among 6813 patients, 4246 (62%) were urban, 2092 (31%) regional, and 475 (7%) remote. Twelve-month all-cause mortality did not differ by rurality (urban: 211 [5.0%]; regional: 103 [4.9%]; remote: 23 [4.8%]; {chi}2=0.991, log-rank P=0.929), a finding confirmed in multivariable analysis. At the time of TAVR, regional and remote patients were younger, more comorbid, had more severe AS, and lower STS scores than urban counterparts. Clinical frailty score, non-transfemoral access, STS score, atrial fibrillation or flutter, and moderate-severe chronic lung disease independently predicted 12-month mortality. Interpretation TAVR outcomes were comparable between rurality groups, suggesting equitable care within Queensland's centralised TAVR model. However, registry data only captures patients who underwent TAVR and may miss older rural patients facing barriers to AS diagnosis, referral, or procedural workup. Funding There was no funding or sponsor involvement.

papers.title: Clinical Usefulness of Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Electrocardiography for Pulmonary Hypertension Detection: A Meta-analysis Based on Pre- and Post-Test Probability
papers.abstract: Pulmonary hypertension is frequently diagnosed late because its early manifestations are nonspecific. Artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography may provide a scalable method for identifying patients who warrant further evaluation. We searched eight databases from inception through May 2026 without language restrictions for studies evaluating artificial intelligence or machine-learning algorithms applied to standard 12-lead electrocardiograms against invasive hemodynamic or echocardiographic reference standards. Two reviewers independently selected studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. Sensitivity and specificity were pooled using a bivariate random-effects model. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251149532). Five retrospective studies comprising 103,884 individuals were included. Pooled sensitivity was 0.81 (95% CI, 0.79-0.82), pooled specificity was 0.80 (95% CI, 0.76-0.83), and the summary area under the curve was 0.85 (95% CI, 0.81-0.88). The positive likelihood ratio was 4.03 (95% CI, 3.38-4.80), and the negative likelihood ratio was 0.24 (95% CI, 0.23-0.26). At a pretest probability of 20%, positive and negative results corresponded to posttest probabilities of approximately 50% and 6%, respectively. Heterogeneity was substantial, but leave-one-out analyses did not materially alter pooled estimates. Artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography showed good performance for detecting pulmonary hypertension and may support targeted case finding. Prospective studies should determine whether its use improves diagnostic pathways and patient outcomes.

papers.title: Implications of the 2026 Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome Guideline for GLP-1 Receptor Agonist and SGLT2 Inhibitor Eligibility Among US Adults
papers.abstract: Background The 2026 cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome guideline broadens recommendations for glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), but the increment over pre-2026 standards is unknown. We estimated the number and clinical profile of US adults newly eligible under this guideline. Methods Cross-sectional analysis of adults aged 30-79 years in the 2011-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Adults were newly eligible if they met 2026 CKM guideline indications but not pre-2026 American Diabetes Association, American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association heart failure, Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes, or obesity guideline indications. Sensitivity analyses used 2 US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) label standards. Results Among 175.17 million US adults, 111.84 million (63.8%) were already eligible for either class. The CKM guideline added 7.48 million (95% CI: 6.48 to 8.47), a 6.7% increase, all for GLP-1RA and none for SGLT2i: 6.49 million with overweight (body mass index 27.0-29.9 kg/m2, ethnicity adjusted) and no other cardiometabolic disease, and 0.99 million with type 2 diabetes and 10-year PREVENT cardiovascular risk ?7.5%. Newly eligible adults (86.8% CKM stage 1) were younger (46.2 vs 52.9 years), leaner (27.8 vs 33.0 kg/m2), and at lower 10- and 30-year PREVENT risk (3.6% vs 8.1%; 11.3% vs 19.6%; all P < 0.001). Against FDA labeling, 14.15-25.17 million were newly eligible (7.66-18.20 million for SGLT2i). Assuming a 20% relative risk reduction, the projected number needed to treat per cardiovascular event prevented was 243 over 10 years and 56 over 30 years (ages 30-59) in adults with overweight, versus 61 and 26 in already eligible adults. Conclusions Relative to pre-2026 society guidelines, the 2026 CKM guideline newly confers a GLP-1RA indication on 7.48 million US adults, predominantly at lower cardiovascular risk. Whether treating these adults improves outcomes in a cost-efficient manner remains to be established.

papers.title: Diastolic Dysfunction Predicts Cardiorespiratory Fitness and Clinical Outcomes in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
papers.abstract: Background. Echocardiographic indices of diastolic dysfunction are routinely obtained in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), but their relationships with cardiorespiratory fitness and long-term clinical outcomes remain poorly defined. Objectives. This study therefore sought to determine the extent to which E/e', left atrial volume index (LAVi), and peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity (TRVmax) relate to peak oxygen uptake, ventilatory efficiency, their longitudinal trajectories, and clinical outcomes in HCM. Methods. We retrospectively studied patients with HCM who completed cardiopulmonary exercise testing within 7 days of resting echocardiography. Each diastolic index was related to percent-predicted peak oxygen uptake (VO2), ventilatory efficiency (VE/VCO2 slope), their serial trajectories, and a composite of heart failure hospitalization, transplantation, or death. Results. Among 441 patients with HCM (mean age 49 +/- 16 years; 66% men), each SD higher E/e', LAVi, and TRVmax was independently associated with lower peak VO2 (-6.0, -3.6, and -6.3 percentage points of predicted) and higher VE/VCO2 slope (+0.9, +1.0, and +2.5; all P <= 0.045), nonlinearly for E/e' with peak VO2 and LAVi with VE/VCO2 slope. On serial testing, only LAVi predicted progressively worsening VE/VCO2 slope (+0.4/yr/SD; 95% CI: 0.13-0.68; P = 0.005). Over a median of 4.8 years, 118 of 436 patients (27.1%) reached the composite endpoint, for which LAVi was the strongest echocardiographic predictor (adjusted HR: 1.68/SD; 95% CI: 1.40-2.03). Conclusions. In HCM, resting diastolic indices were associated with cardiorespiratory fitness, and higher LAVi was independently associated with a steeper rise in VE/VCO2 slope and heart failure events. Resting diastolic phenotyping may complement exercise testing.

papers.title: Cholesterol Paradox: Multi-point Heart Failure Prediction from Lipid Panels in Electronic Health Records
papers.abstract: In cardiovascular medicine, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is the main lipid marker used in routine screening to assess cardiovascular risk and guide preventive treatment and dietary changes. An increasing number of studies have recently documented the cholesterol paradox: patients with or at risk of heart failure (HF) often have unexpectedly low levels of LDL-C despite leading to cardiovascular diseases. This paper examines how well retrospective lipid panel measurements, supplemented with apolipoprotein B (ApoB), can predict an initial heart failure (HF) event in several pre-diagnosis time windows, using age-matched patient data from Electronic Health Records (EHRs). This retrospective study uses lipid profiles from multicenter nationwide EHRs from the All of Us Research Program. We apply machine learning and explainable AI (SHAP) to lipid-based prediction and to interpret cholesterol contributions to the diagnosis of first heart failure (HF). One experiment predicts the diagnosis of HF in 36 months; the other distinguishes HF patients from people who have never been diagnosed with cardiovascular disease. A baseline lipid panel that includes ApoB predicts the first HF event up to 36 months in advance, achieving an AUC of 0.624 in men and 0.627 in women. Compared to a group of the same age without previous cardiovascular disease, a lipid profile including ApoB predicts a first HF event with a substantially higher AUC: 0.937 for men and 0.925 for women. Shapley value analyses suggest that higher triglycerides and lower HDL and LDL levels are linked to subsequent HF events, with LDL appearing as the strongest yet counterintuitive predictor. ApoB ranks second in importance; in males, higher ApoB is associated with a greater risk of HF, unlike LDL. In general, the study highlights an unexpected association with LDL and emphasizes the prognostic utility of sex-specific metabolic indicators (TG, HDL) for HF using routinely collected clinical data.

papers.title: Repeat Hospitalizations and Their Costs in the 6 Months After Acute Myocarditis
papers.abstract: BackgroundReadmission metrics after acute myocarditis usually record only whether the first readmission occurs within 30 days. The amount of inpatient care received after the first return and the period over which it was received are unknown. MethodsWe identified adults with a principal diagnosis of acute myocarditis (ICD-10-CM I40.x) in the Nationwide Readmission Database (NRD) from 2016 to 2022. The first qualifying admission in each patient year served as the index, and patients had to be discharged alive and not transferred. We linked every subsequent same-state, same-year admission for any cause within 30, 90, and 180 days. Using survey-weighted methods, we split the return length of stay (LOS) and estimated hospital cost (charges x cost-to-charge ratio, 2022 US dollars) into first-return and beyond-first-return components per index patient; patients without readmission were counted as having zero. The National Inpatient Sample (NIS) provided data on index mortality and costs. ResultsOf the 3,276 sampled index patients eligible for the 180-day follow-up (5,897 for 30 days), 6.5% were readmitted within 30 days and 14.0% within 180 days. Over 180 days, readmissions added 1.51 (95% CI, 1.23-1.79) bed-days and $5,884 (95% CI, 4,352-7,417) per index patient. Readmissions after the first contributed 0.62 (0.42-0.82) days and $2,430 (1,599-3,262), which is 41% of return bed-days and 41% of return costs (95% CI, 34-49 and 33-49, respectively). Counting only the first readmission, therefore, understated the 180-day return burden by 1.7-fold. The beyond-first share rose from 10% at 30 days to 32% at 90 days and 41% at 180 days, and 63% of the 180-day return bed-days accrued after day 30. Most readmissions had a non-cardiovascular (55% of bed-days) or other cardiovascular (33%) principal diagnosis, and myocarditis accounted for 3.5%. In the NIS (2,964 admissions; 71 in-hospital deaths), survivors had a mean index LOS of 4.4 days and a mean cost of $23,867. ConclusionsAfter acute myocarditis, approximately two-fifths of the 6-month readmission bed-days and costs were from second and later readmissions. Most accrued after the usual 30-day window and were diagnoses other than myocarditis. First-readmission 30-day metrics substantially understate the post-discharge hospital burden in this population cohort. What Is Known- Hospitalization for acute myocarditis carries a substantial risk of early readmission; national studies have reported 30- or 90-day readmission rates. - Hospital quality and cost metrics typically consider only the first readmission within 30 days of discharge. What the Study AddsIn a nationally representative US cohort, 41% of 180-day readmission bed-days and costs after acute myocarditis came from second and later readmissions; first-readmission metrics understated the 180- day return burden 1.7-fold. Nearly two-thirds of the 180-day return bed-days occurred after day 30, and almost 9 in 10 were for diagnoses other than myocarditis, heart failure, or arrhythmia. These findings support follow-up that extends beyond 30 days and address coexisting conditions.

papers.title: ECG-Derived Synthetic Left Ventricular Mechanics Predict Mortality After Acute Myocardial Infarction and Fatal Myocardial Infarction in the General Population
papers.abstract: BackgroundLeft ventricular (LV) mechanical function predicts outcomes after acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Recovering these parameters from the 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) could enable point-of-care risk assessment wherever an ECG is acquired. ObjectivesTo determine whether ECG-derived synthetic LV mechanics predict all-cause mortality after AMI and myocardial infarction (MI)-specific mortality in the general population and add information beyond the GRACE score and ejection fraction. MethodsSynthetic peak systolic (s') and early diastolic (e') mitral annular velocities and mitral annular plane systolic excursion (MAPSE) were derived from the 12-lead ECG by a previously validated generative adversarial network, applied without retraining and blinded to outcome. Associations were assessed in an AMI cohort (n=1,065) by Cox regression and a population cohort (n=219,564) by Fine-Gray models. Incremental value was tested against GRACE, three AI-ECG reduced ejection fraction (EF) models, and measured LVEF. ResultsIn the AMI cohort (109 deaths; median follow-up 1.44 years), all three parameters predicted all-cause mortality (each P<0.001). Synthetic e' was the sole independent predictor after adjustment for clinical covariates (HR=0.90 per 1 cm/s; 95% CI 0.84-0.98) and for GRACE (HR=0.90; 0.83-0.97; P=0.006). In the post-discharge cohort (n=1,017; 61 deaths), synthetic e' improved discrimination beyond GRACE (C-index 0.67 to 0.70; HR=0.84 per 1 cm/s; 95% CI 0.76-0.93; P=0.001) and remained independent of AI-ECG-predicted and measured LVEF (HR 0.84-0.86 per 1 cm/s; all P[≤]0.004), contributing 28-46% of each models prognostic information. In the population cohort (817 MI deaths; median follow-up 3.42 years), all three predicted MI-specific mortality after adjustment for age, sex, and ECG abnormalities, MAPSE showing the largest effect (sHR=0.49; 95% CI 0.37-0.65), with s' (sHR=0.78; 0.72-0.84) and e' (sHR=0.87; 0.82-0.93) also predictive (each P<0.001). ConclusionsECG-derived synthetic LV mechanical parameters predict all-cause mortality after AMI and fatal MI in the general population, adding information beyond the GRACE score and LVEF.

papers.title: Patient-specific finite element modeling of image-derived shell morphoelastic growth: A general framework and application to stented aortic dissection
papers.abstract: Vascular pathology often manifests in complex shape evolution visualized by longitudinal computed tomography (CT) imaging. Growth and remodeling (G&R) frameworks have been integrated into finite element (FE) modeling to probe the mechanics underlying this progression, extending into patient-specific approaches. Their scalability and translatability, however, are limited by the computational burden associated with heterogeneous, anisotropic growth fields and through-thickness meshing. While existing shell growth formulations can mitigate this burden, they require nontrivial FE implementation especially in commercial softwares (e.g., Abaqus) and their efficacy in patient-specific geometries under complex loading is unclear. In this work, we present a general computational framework to implement shell morphoelastic growth computed directly from registered patient-specific CT images. This shell implementation is validated against solid 3D formulations, allows thickness tunability, and increases compatibility with CT surfaces. We demonstrate the robustness of this formulation through modeling post-operative growth in a patient-specific aortic dissection under stent-based loading. Results first show that complex stent-based loading can deform the shell dissection flap to reproduce post-operative geometry. The outer aortic wall is then given a growth field calculated from registration of 1-month and 5-year post-operative CT images, which is implemented along with stent-based loading and pressurization. Results from this model capture the trends in total and lumen morphological evolution observed at intermediate timepoints. These findings establish a general framework, validated with a patient-specific case study of aortic dissection, with the potential to expand to other complex systems, scale to larger patient populations, and apply G&R to clinical translation.

papers.title: Impact of Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Burden on Echocardiographic Remodeling and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Hypertension
papers.abstract: AimsCardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome highlights the interrelationship between metabolic, renal, and cardiovascular disorders. However, whether CKM burden influences longitudinal cardiac structural and functional recovery and subsequent cardiovascular outcomes remains unclear. MethodsWe studied 1,600 patients from the STRATS-HHD registry who underwent echocardiography at baseline and 6-18 months after treatment initiation. CKM burden was defined by obesity, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and severe hypertension (0-1, 2, or [≥]3 components). The primary outcome was cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization (HHF). ResultsCKM burden was 0-1 in 973 patients (60.8%), 2 in 440 (27.5%), and [≥]3 in 187 (11.7%). Higher burden was associated with worse baseline cardiac abnormalities and increased primary outcome risk (adjusted HR, 3.09; 95% CI, 1.92-4.98 for [≥]3 vs 0-1; adjusted HR, 1.53; 95% CI, 1.27-1.84 per +1 CKM component). The prognostic association persisted after additional adjustment for hepatic steatosis index-defined metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. Despite overall improvement in most echocardiographic parameters after treatment, patients with CKM burden [≥]3 showed less favorable E/e', LV global longitudinal strain (GLS), and LA stiffness index at follow-up. Normalization of these parameters at follow-up was associated with substantially lower subsequent cardiovascular risk. Mediation analyses suggested that echocardiographic abnormalities partially mediated the association between high CKM burden and the primary outcome. ConclusionCKM burden identifies hypertensive patients with less favorable cardiac function after treatment and increased cardiovascular risk. These findings highlight the association of CKM burden with cardiac functional recovery and prognosis in patients with hypertension. Graphical AbstractIn patients with hypertension, higher CKM burden was associated with more pronounced cardiac abnormalities, less favorable cardiac functional status after antihypertensive treatment, and increased cardiovascular risk. Normalization of functional echocardiographic parameters was associated with lower subsequent cardiovascular risk. papers.title: Membrane theory with multimodal evidence defines blood pressure measurement
papers.abstract: Cuff-based blood pressure (BP) measurement is a cornerstone of health assessment, yet its mechanism remains unclear and measurement error remains substantial1. On the basis of membrane theory2,3, we propose that external pressure generated by cuff inflation follows a hyperbolic-cosine-shaped axial distribution along the artery, forming a pressure-peak zone (PPZ) beneath the cuff. By combining this external pressure with intra-arterial pressure, we constructed a mathematical model that systematically predicts site-specific vascular motion and hemodynamic changes during BP measurement. In humans, multimodal experiments integrating vascular imaging and synchronized invasive and noninvasive pressure measurements validated the model. The PPZ organizes distinct proximal and distal hemodynamics during cuff pressurization: at DBP, diastolic arterial collapse begins at the PPZ; near SBP, only weak residual blood flow traverses the PPZ and disappears once cuff pressure exceeds SBP. These transitions generated identifiable oscillogram features for DBP and SBP, precisely localized by wavelet scanning. The resulting method showed higher accuracy and lower variability than auscultation and conventional oscillometry and was the only method whose estimates did not differ significantly from invasive BP. This study redefines the hemodynamic basis of cuff-based BP measurement, and its mechanistic framework and accuracy may support clinical application and more reliable therapeutic decision-making. Structured AbstractO_ST_ABSIntroductionC_ST_ABSBrachial cuff-based noninvasive blood pressure (BP) measurement is among the most important measurements in medicine, yet its underlying mechanism remains unclear. Current oscillometric and auscultatory techniques rely largely on empirical criteria and show substantial errors and variability when compared with invasive BP. A core theoretical basis is therefore needed to link cuff-vessel coupling mechanics to hemodynamic changes and to support a more accurate, mechanism-consistent method for BP estimation. RationaleTraditional cuff-based BP theories assume vascular compression due to a spatially uniform external force. These theories cannot explain prior observations: tourniquet studies using cuffs similar to BP cuffs showed axial central tissue injury; intratissue pressure measurements and direct measurements of cuff contact pressure all showed curvilinear axial pressure distributions. Because the cuff is intrinsically a membrane structure, we hypothesized that sub-cuff pressure distribution should follow a membrane-theory contact model and a Laplace-type equilibrium. By combining this nonuniform external pressure with intra-arterial pressure, we constructed and validated a mathematical model that systematically predicts vascular motion, hemodynamics, and oscillogram changes during BP measurement. ResultsThe model predicted that the cuff external pressure follows a hyperbolic-cosine-like axial distribution, forming a pressure-peak zone (PPZ) at the cuff axial center, the site of minimal curvature, with external pressure decreasing toward proximal and distal edges. Sub-cuff pressure-sensor measurements and transvenous tissue-pressure measurements in supine participants verified this pressure-distribution pattern and showed that, once cuff pressure exceeded approximately 30 mmHg, cuff pressure and tissue pressure in the PPZ were nearly identical. On this mechanistic basis, we established a physically constrained mathematical framework that reproduced vascular motion and hemodynamic changes during inflation and linked vascular dynamics to oscillogram morphology. Angiography, intravascular ultrasound (IVUS), computed tomographic angiography (CTA), and multisite invasive pressure measurements in the human brachial artery showed that the model-predicted motion, hemodynamics, multisite pressure, cross-sectional area, volume, and oscillogram changes agreed with measured results. The arterial PPZ was the primary site determining key state transitions of the sub-cuff vessel and the dominant contributor to hemodynamic and oscillogram changes. When cuff pressure rose above diastolic blood pressure (DBP) during inflation, the PPZ first collapsed during diastole, gradually creating two regions with distinct vascular motion proximal and distal to the PPZ. Near systolic blood pressure (SBP), distal pulsations became markedly delayed and attenuated into distinctive low-amplitude delayed pulsations (small waves). When cuff pressure exceeded SBP, pulsations in the PPZ and distal region disappeared, whereas proximal pulsations persisted. These hemodynamic events mapped onto characteristic oscillogram morphology transitions. Using wavelet scanning analysis, we extracted local oscillatory components as reference features for SBP and DBP. Auscultation, vascular imaging, and synchronized pressure recordings during the cardiac cycle showed that Korotkoff sounds (KS) occurred during early vascular opening and were related to expansion velocity. Our model further allowed estimation of the area-derived expansion velocity near the distal cuff edge; however, KS-generation thresholds vary across individuals. When cuff pressure is close to SBP, weak blood passage produces expansion velocities below the KS threshold, causing systematic underestimation. In contrast, near DBP, mild post-collapse re-expansion may trigger KS prematurely or with delay, leading to substantial variability. The model also showed that the conventional oscillometric amplitude-coefficient method for estimating SBP and DBP can be analytically derived from our mathematical equations. However, because these parameters are numerous and case-specific, they cannot be practically determined; therefore, the maximum amplitude algorithm (MAA) must rely on empirical ratios relative to the maximum oscillogram amplitude. Consequently, MAA exhibits not only systematic bias but also substantial variability. On the basis of this mechanism, we developed the novel Morphology-Transition Oscillometry (MTO) method for noninvasive BP measurement. For SBP, MTO showed consistently much higher accuracy and lower dispersion in 175 participants (0.39 {+/-} 6.41 mmHg) than conventional auscultation (KS) (-6.58 {+/-} 10.30 mmHg) and oscillometry based on MAA (-6.79 {+/-} 10.58 mmHg), with no significant difference from invasive pressure. For DBP, the bias was 0.14 {+/-} 6.25 mmHg for MTO, -1.15 {+/-} 7.24 mmHg for KS, and 4.85 {+/-} 9.14 mmHg for MAA. ConclusionThis membrane-theory-based framework establishes a reliable new theory of cuff-based BP measurement, accurately predicting hemodynamic transitions, vascular motion, and oscillogram morphology, as validated by multimodal in vivo measurements. The MTO method derived from this theory measured arterial BP more accurately than auscultation and traditional oscillometry.

papers.title: Acute Changes in Left Atrial Appendage Flow Velocity During Pulsed Field Ablation: An Intraprocedural Intracardiac Echocardiography Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundDespite the close anatomical relationship between the left pulmonary veins (PVs) and the left atrial appendage (LAA), acute changes in LAA flow during pulsed field ablation (PFA) remain poorly characterized. ObjectivesTo characterize acute intraprocedural changes in LAA flow and transmitral filling during PFA for atrial fibrillation (AF) using paired intracardiac echocardiography (ICE). MethodsPatients with paroxysmal or persistent AF undergoing PFA were prospectively enrolled if they were in sinus rhythm at the beginning of the procedure. ICE was performed immediately before and after PFA to assess LAA emptying velocity (LAAEv), LAA filling velocity (LAAFv), transmitral E- and A-wave velocities, and E-wave deceleration time (EDT). Paired pre-to-post PFA changes were assessed, followed by a sensitivity analysis using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) and exploratory subgroup analyses. ResultsAmong 98 patients, LAAEv increased from 35.45 to 40.00 cm/s immediately after PFA (estimated paired increase, 4.95 cm/s; 95% CI, 2.35-7.80; P<0.001), while LAAFv increased by 4.36 cm/s (95% CI, 1.81-6.91; P=0.001). E-wave velocity increased by 8.69 cm/s and EDT decreased by 31.73 ms (both P<0.001), whereas A-wave velocity did not change significantly (P=0.08). In the ANCOVA model, changes in heart rate, systolic blood pressure, and vasopressor use were not significantly associated with changes in LAAEv. A marked acute reduction in LAAEv ([≥]20%) occurred in 12 patients (12.2%). No significant subgroup interactions were observed. ConclusionsLAA flow velocities increased acutely after PFA, accompanied by changes in transmitral filling, although a minority of patients showed a marked acute reduction in LAA emptying.

papers.title: Reporting of Pericardial Adverse Events with Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors: A Disproportionality Analysis of the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System
papers.abstract: BackgroundImmune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) can cause immune-related adverse events in almost any organ. While myocarditis has received the most attention, data on pericardial disease with ICI use are limited. We examined pericardial adverse event reporting with nine ICIs using the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS). MethodsWe combined legacy AERS and current FAERS quarterly files from January 2011 to June 2026 into 18,629,240 unique cases, deduplicated by case number, and removed cases the FDA had listed as deleted. ICI exposure was identified from generic names, brand names, development code names and the active-ingredient field. Pericardial events were defined by seven MedDRA preferred terms. We estimated reporting odds ratios (ROR), proportional reporting ratios (PRR), Bayesian information components (IC) and empirical Bayes geometric means (EBGM). We also examined myocarditis co-reporting, time trends, a comparison with other antineoplastic agents, a MedDRA query-based outcome, and 14 alternative definitions. ResultsThe analysis included 18,514,045 cases: 277,434 involved an ICI, 34,792 carried a pericardial term, and 1,680 had both. Pericardial events were reported disproportionately with ICIs (ROR 3.35 (95% CI 3.19 to 3.52); PRR 3.34; IC025 1.62). Eight of nine agents had a ROR above 1 (3.32 to 5.63). Among the most frequently reported terms, estimates were highest for cardiac tamponade (5.59 (95% CI 4.98 to 6.28)), followed by pericardial effusion (3.83 (95% CI 3.60 to 4.07)) and pericarditis (2.09 (95% CI 1.89 to 2.31)). After removing cases that also reported myocarditis, the ROR was 3.13 (95% CI 2.98 to 3.30). Most sensitivity analyses gave similar estimates (ROR 3.13 to 3.47); defining exposure by generic drug names alone, which identified only 44% of exposed cases, gave 3.99. Compared with cases naming other L01 antineoplastic agents, the ROR was 1.13 (95% CI 1.08 to 1.19): 1.28 (95% CI 1.20 to 1.36) for ICI-only cases and 0.96 (95% CI 0.89 to 1.04) when another antineoplastic was also named. The ICI-specific reporting odds ratio fell each quarter (odds ratio 0.977 per quarter, 95% CI 0.973 to 0.980). ConclusionsIn FAERS, pericardial events were reported more often with ICIs than with other drugs across most agents and terms; however, incidence and causation cannot be determined. The excess over other antineoplastic agents was small, and reporting disproportionality declined over time. These findings support clinical awareness of pericardial disease in patients receiving ICIs and warrant study in data that can measure incidence.

papers.title: Plantar Thermography for Longitudinal Remote Monitoring of Chronic Heart Failure
papers.abstract: Rural patients with heart failure (HF) have poor access to care, worse outcomes, and may benefit from at-home monitoring. We evaluated whether foot temperature measured using a thermographic floor mat was associated with invasively measured cardiac output and whether longitudinal temperature changes preceded HF events. We conducted a two-part prospective, observational single-center study using the SmartMat (Podimetrics, Somerville, MA), which acquires plantar thermograms and ambient temperature. In the acute study, patients undergoing clinically indicated right heart catheterization completed 4 scans on the same day. In the chronic study, patients with a HF hospitalization in the past year and New York Heart Association Class II-III symptoms were instructed to use the device and a scale daily for 6 months. A HF event was defined as receiving at least one dose of intravenous or subcutaneous diuretic. Thirty patients were enrolled in the acute study. Mean right hallux temperature positively correlated with thermodilution cardiac output (r=0.63, p<0.001). 42 patients were enrolled in the chronic study. Among patients experiencing an HF event, ambient-adjusted hallux temperature declined in the 15 days immediately preceding the event compared with days 15- 30 before the event. Plantar thermograms are associated with invasively measured cardiac output and may detect subclinical worsening before HF events. Foot temperature may provide complementary information regarding HF decompensation, supporting further evaluation of plantar thermography for remote HF monitoring.

papers.title: Fully Automated Multi-Chamber Strain Profiling in Consecutive Patients Undergoing Transthoracic Echocardiography: Feasibility, Functional Clustering, and Prognostic Implications
papers.abstract: AimsMyocardial strain enables sensitive assessment of cardiac function, but its clinical application has largely focused on individual chambers or selected patient populations. We evaluated the feasibility and clinical relevance of fully automated multi-chamber strain assessment in consecutive patients undergoing routine transthoracic echocardiography (TTE). Methods and resultsThis retrospective study included 8,350 consecutive adults undergoing TTE. A hospital-wide artificial intelligence (AI)-based system automatically measured left ventricular (LV) global longitudinal strain (LVGLS), left atrial (LA) reservoir strain (LASr), and right ventricular (RV) free-wall strain (RVFWS). AI-derived LVGLS was available from at least one apical view in 97.1% of patients and from all three views in 94.8%; LASr and RVFWS were available in 94.1% and 94.5%, respectively, resulting in complete multi-chamber strain assessment in 90.3%. Strain measures showed modest correlations with conventional chamber-specific echocardiographic parameters and differential associations with clinical outcomes. Gaussian mixture modeling identified three distinct clusters characterized by preserved multi-chamber function, RV-dominant dysfunction, and pan-chamber dysfunction. papers.title: Cardiac MRI at 3.0T in the presence of implantable cardioverter defibrillators (ICDs)
papers.abstract: Patients with implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) often are excluded from receiving CMR scans at 3.0T due to ICD-induced image artifacts. This work aims to transfer sequence protocols established for CMR imaging in the presence of ICDs at 1.5T to a first human application at 3.0T. All measurements were performed on a clinical 3T MRI scanner. Phantom measurements were used to establish and optimize wideband PSIR LGE imaging at 3.0T. Volunteer measurements with externally placed ICDs were used for optimization of CINE imaging and wideband PSIR imaging. Thirdly, patients with implanted ICD were examined with the optimized protocols. Human measurements showed that SA stacks obtained with spoiled GRE after contrast agent showed a markedly lower artifact burden than the conventional approach. For scar imaging, a wideband PSIR with a bandwidth of 3kHz and a frequency offset of +750Hz allowed a sufficient suppression of relevant artifacts in the majority of scans. No strong correlation between the image quality and the distance between the cardiac silhouette and the device was detected. The presented work shows the feasibility of clinical cardiac MRI at 3.0T including GRE-CINE and wideband PSIR-LGE for patients with ICDs.

papers.title: Left Ventricular Diastolic Intraventricular Pressure Differences and Propagation Velocity with 4D-Flow MRI in Patients with Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
papers.abstract: BackgroundTransthoracic echocardiography (TTE) remains the gold standard for assessing left ventricular (LV) diastolic dysfunction (DD), but noninvasive alternatives are needed to overcome geometric and acoustic limitations. 4D-Flow MRI enables comprehensive assessment of intraventricular pressure differences (IVPDs) and flow propagation velocity (VP). We aimed to evaluate 4D-Flow-derived IVPDs and VP in patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). MethodsThirty-eight HCM patients and 38 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent TTE and 4D-Flow MRI. Spatiotemporal maps of velocity and IVPDs, decomposed into inertial and convective components, were derived along the main inflow streamline from the mitral valve to the apex. Peak early filling rate (PEFR) was used to normalize IVPDs and VP. papers.title: Prevalence and Clinical Correlates of Coronary Perivascular Inflammation in an Asymptomatic Adult Primary Prevention Population: An Assessment of the CT-Derived Fat Attenuation Index Score (FAI-Score)
papers.abstract: BackgroundCoronary perivascular fat attenuation index score (FAI-Score) on coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) quantifies vascular inflammation and predicts cardiac mortality in symptomatic cohorts. However, its prevalence, anatomical distribution, and clinical correlates in asymptomatic primary prevention populations remain uncharacterized. MethodsIn an IRB-approved prospective study across two clinical sites, 84 consecutive asymptomatic adults (mean age 53.7 {+/-} 8.6 years; 63.1% men) with no prior coronary artery disease underwent screening CCTA and comprehensive clinical, metabolic, and biomarker profiling. AI-standardized FAI-Score was quantified across three epicardial vessels (LAD, LCx, RCA). High and very high perivascular inflammation were pre-specified as any vessel [≥]75th and [≥]90th percentiles, respectively. Luminal stenosis and plaque were graded using CAD-RADS 2.0. ResultsElevated FAI-Score ([≥]75th percentile) was present in 42.9% of participants (36/84; 95% CI 32.8% - 53.5%), with 17.9% (15/84; 95% CI 11.1% - 27.4%) exhibiting very high inflammation ([≥]90th percentile). Multi-vessel inflammation was identified in 17.9% (15/84), with the RCA most frequently involved ([≥]90th percentile in 13.1%). Standard circulating biomarkers, including ApoB, non-HDL-C, HbA1c, and PREVENT-ASCVD 10-year risk showed no association with binary inflammation. Systemic hs-CRP (median 0.8 mg/L) exhibited an inverse correlation with maximum vessel FAI-Score (Spearman {rho}=-0.27, p=0.014). Men demonstrated higher rates of elevated FAI-Score than women (52.8% vs. 25.8%, p=0.016; [≥]90th percentile: 26.4% vs. 3.2%, p=0.007). Strikingly, 46.2% (30/65) of participants with normal luminal anatomy (CAD-RADS 0) and 47.2% (25/53) with zero plaque burden harbored elevated FAI-Score; all 15 individuals with very high FAI-Score had CAD-RADS 0 (Fishers exact p=0.018). Body mass index was the sole secondary correlate surviving false discovery rate correction (AUC = 0.71, p=0.001, all-test FDR q=0.028). Regularized multivariable models showed modest out-of-sample discrimination for FAI-Score elevation (cross-validated AUC = 0.71). ConclusionsCoronary perivascular inflammation is common among asymptomatic adults and frequently uncouples from structural plaque and luminal stenosis. Routine circulating biomarkers and clinical risk calculators fail to identify inflamed vessels, highlighting FAI-Score as an independent dimension of primary cardiovascular risk assessment.

papers.title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Clinical Profile, Diagnosis, and Outcomes of Cardiac Amyloidosis in Cali, Colombia
papers.abstract: BackgroundCardiac amyloidosis is an increasingly recognized cause of heart failure in older adults, yet data from Colombia and, in particular, from the countrys southwest region remain scarce. We describe the clinical, diagnostic, imaging, and outcome profile of patients with cardiac amyloidosis at two high-complexity institutions in Cali. MethodsObservational, descriptive, retrospective, two-center study. Patients were identified through the institutional registries of both centers using ICD-10 diagnostic codes for amyloidosis, and clinical information was collected manually from medical records. Continuous variables are reported as median (interquartile range) and categorical variables as counts and percentages, with the number of patients with available data specified for each variable. ResultsThirty-two patients were analyzed (median age 77 years; 68.8% men). Heart failure was nearly universal (90.6%) and atrial fibrillation was frequent (46.9%); carpal tunnel syndrome was present in 31.2%. Bone scintigraphy showed positive myocardial uptake (Perugini 2-3) in 88.5%, and the Val142Ile variant was found in all genotyped patients, consistent with a predominance of transthyretin amyloidosis. Left ventricular ejection fraction was preserved in most patients despite marked concentric hypertrophy. Tafamidis was used in 37.5%. Overall mortality was 35.5%, and NT-proBNP was markedly higher among patients who died (median 6640 vs 1186 pg/mL; p=0.003). ConclusionsIn this southwest Colombian cohort, cardiac amyloidosis presented as the classic transthyretin phenotype of the older male with hypertrophic, non-dilated heart failure, a high yield of non-invasive diagnosis, and a striking predominance of the Val142Ile variant. Mortality was high and closely linked to NT-proBNP.

papers.title: Preoperative Systemic Immune-Inflammation Index and Clinical Outcomes After Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) is a routinely available blood-derived marker with potential prognostic relevance after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). We evaluated associations between preoperative SII and postoperative outcomes. MethodsPubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science were searched to 1 October 2026, with supplementary searches through 14 October 2026. Peer-reviewed observational studies evaluating preoperative SII in adults undergoing CABG were eligible. Methodological quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Compatible categorical associations and exploratory adjusted continuous mortality effects were pooled separately using restricted maximum-likelihood random-effects models; other findings were summarized descriptively. ResultsThirty-one reports were included, with an aggregate sample of 30,976 and possible cohort overlap; five contributed to meta-analysis. Two off-pump cohorts comprising 1,378 patients and 180 atrial-fibrillation events yielded an imprecise crude association with postoperative atrial fibrillation (OR 1.60, 95%CI 0.53-4.82; I2=68%). An exploratory crude synthesis indicated greater intra-aortic balloon pump use with higher SII (OR 2.45, 95%CI 1.16-5.18; I2=51%). Two cohorts with differing follow-up yielded an exploratory adjusted mortality HR of 1.11 (95% Wald CI 1.05-1.18) per study-specific SD increase in log-SII. In one 624-patient cohort, high SII was associated with postoperative acute kidney injury after adjustment (OR 3.35, 95% CI 2.25-4.97).Apparent atrial-fibrillation discrimination varied (AUC 0.587-0.946). ConclusionsPreoperative SII showed associations with selected adverse outcomes after CABG, supporting further evaluation as an accessible prognostic marker. Its incremental value beyond established clinical risk models requires validation.

papers.title: Teaching an ECG model where to look does not make it more robust to missing leads: a pre-registered comparison of guideline-based attention guidance with random lead masking
papers.abstract: BackgroundReal-world 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs) often have missing or corrupted leads. A deep-learning classifier can be prepared for this by random lead masking during training, or by injecting clinical knowledge, for example by pulling its attention towards the leads that guidelines use for each diagnosis. Whether this knowledge adds robustness beyond masking is unknown. MethodsPre-registered comparison of three arms sharing one network (per-lead 1D-ResNet encoder and per-diagnosis attention over the 12 leads): standard training (M0); random whole-lead masking (M1); masking plus a Kullback-Leibler penalty pulling attention towards a fixed guideline-derived key-lead map (M2, guideline-based attention guidance). Six diagnoses; five seeds per arm. Development on PTB-XL (21,799 ECGs); single sealed evaluation on PTB-XL fold 10 (2,198 ECGs) and on CODE-15% (233,204 exams, external validation). Primary endpoint: AUROC difference M2 - M1, averaged over first-degree AV block, right and left bundle branch block and atrial fibrillation and over 1 to 6 lost (zeroed) leads, with a patient-level paired BCa bootstrap 95% confidence interval. ResultsThe guidance did not change robustness: {Delta}AUROC -0.0010 (95% CI -0.0033 to +0.0006), an interval entirely within the pre-specified {+/-}0.02 margin; the result was unchanged with another bootstrap seed, other interval methods and leave-one-diagnosis-out analyses. Masking improved AUROC: M1 - M0 = +0.0134 (95% CI +0.0102 to +0.0172) when one key lead was lost, and the number of lost leads tolerated before AUROC fell by more than 0.02 rose from 7 (M0) to 10 (M1). M2 attention matched the map and M2 was non-inferior on intact ECGs, but its calibration slope was lower for all six diagnoses in both datasets. M2 lost slightly more when all key leads were lost together (-0.0067) and gained only when one to three leads remained (exploratory; AUROC 0.9408 vs 0.9210 with 11 leads lost). CODE-15% reproduced every pattern (primary -0.0007, 95% CI -0.0011 to -0.0003). ConclusionsRandom lead masking suffices to make an ECG classifier robust to missing leads; adding guideline knowledge aligns attention with clinical criteria but adds no robustness and worsens calibration. Guideline-aligned attention should not be taken as evidence of robustness.
